34.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during the Roman occupation of Palestine, at a time when religious and political tensions were high and crucifixion was a common method of execution for criminals.
34.passage: In John 19, we witness the crucifixion of Jesus. This chapter describes the tragic events leading to His death, highlighting the suffering of Christ and the fulfillment of prophecies. Verse 34 brings to light the physical reality of Jesus' death and the spiritual consequences of His sacrifice.
34.culture: In Jewish culture, blood is often associated with life and sacrifice, while water is a symbol of purification and new beginnings. The combination of these two elements in this verse evokes themes of redemption and purification that are central to the Christian faith.
34.interpretation: The water and blood that flow from Jesus' side symbolize the purification and redemption offered by His death. This reminds believers that through Christ's sacrifice, they receive not only the forgiveness of their sins but also eternal life. This passage underscores the importance of faith in Christ to access this new life.
34.commentaire: John 19:34 reminds us of the depth of Jesus' sacrifice and His immeasurable love for humanity. By piercing His side, the soldier reveals the reality of Christ's suffering and the fulfillment of God's promise to save His people. As believers, we are called to meditate on this sacrifice and to live in response to this love, sharing the good news of redemption with those around us.

mots.sens: This word means 'testimony' and comes from the root 'μάρτυς' (martus), which designates a witness. In the context of John 19:35, it emphasizes the importance of the truthfulness and authenticity of the testimony of the one who saw the crucifixion of Jesus. This term has significant theological implications, as it establishes the basis of the Christian faith: believing in the truth of Christ through the testimony of eyewitnesses.

This word means 'true' and is derived from 'ἀλήθεια' (aletheia), which means 'truth'. In this verse, it highlights the reliable and authentic nature of the testimony given. Spiritually, this reminds believers that faith in Christ rests on solid foundations, based on the truth revealed by those who witnessed His life and death.

This term means 'to believe' or 'to have faith'. It implies an active and personal trust in the truth of what is proclaimed. In the context of this verse, it calls readers to respond to the testimony by placing their faith in Jesus, thus emphasizing the importance of personal faith in the relationship with God.

35.epoque: The passage is set in the 1st century, during the period of Roman occupation in Judea, a time of religious and political tension.
35.passage: This verse is part of the account of the crucifixion of Jesus, where the apostle John, an eyewitness, emphasizes the importance of his testimony to encourage the faith of believers.
35.culture: In Jewish culture, the testimony of an eyewitness was crucial to establish the truth, and this is reflected in how John presents his experience as a foundation of the Christian faith.
35.interpretation: This verse reminds us that the Christian faith is based on authentic and verifiable testimonies. John's declaration aims to strengthen the belief of the disciples in the reality of Jesus' crucifixion and resurrection.
35.commentaire: John 19:35 invites us to reflect on the solidity of our faith. By relying on the testimony of eyewitnesses, we are encouraged to believe in the truth of the Gospel. This also reminds us of our responsibility to share our own testimony of how Christ has transformed our lives, so that others may believe.

mots.sens: This word refers to a 'bone' in the physical sense, but in a spiritual context, it symbolizes solidity and durability. In antiquity, bones were often associated with life and resurrection, as they are the structures that support the body. In John 19:36, the absence of broken bones emphasizes the perfection of Christ's sacrifice, which is without flaw and fulfills the Scriptures.

This term means 'prophecy' and refers to a statement made under divine inspiration concerning future events. In the context of John 19:36, it highlights the fulfillment of God's promises through Christ. This reinforces the faith of believers in God's faithfulness to His promises, as every detail of Christ's passion was foretold in the Scriptures.

36.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during the Roman occupation of Palestine, a period marked by religious and political tensions. The Jews were awaiting a Messiah who would liberate their nation and restore their kingdom.
36.passage: John 19 describes the events surrounding the crucifixion of Jesus. Verse 36 refers to the fulfillment of the Scriptures, emphasizing that every detail of Christ's Passion was prophesied and has been faithfully realized.
36.culture: In Jewish culture, respect for the Scriptures and prophecies was fundamental. Rites and sacrifices were central elements of faith, and the preservation of bodies after death was also an important aspect of Mosaic law.
36.interpretation: This verse demonstrates that Jesus is the announced Messiah, whose death and resurrection were planned by God. The absence of broken bones in His body is a sign of His perfection and His role as the Lamb of God, without blemish.
36.commentaire: John 19:36 reminds us that every detail of Jesus' life and death was under divine control. This encourages us to trust in God's sovereignty in our own lives, knowing that He fulfills His promises. As we meditate on Christ's suffering, we are called to recognize the importance of His sacrifice and to live in response to this immeasurable love.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to have' or 'to possess'. In the context of John 19:37, it is used to express the possession of a deep spiritual reality. The root of the word evokes the idea of maintaining or keeping something, which underscores the importance of the vision of Christ for those who have pierced Him. Theologically, this refers to the recognition of Jesus as the suffering Messiah, whose sacrifice is essential for the salvation of humanity.

This term means 'to surround' or 'to encircle', but in a more metaphorical sense, it can also evoke the idea of protection or inclusion. In this verse, it emphasizes how those who have pierced Christ are ultimately surrounded by divine grace and mercy. This reminds us that even those who caused Jesus' suffering can be touched by His redemption.

This verb means 'to see' or 'to perceive'. In the context of John 19:37, it implies a spiritual vision that goes beyond mere physical observation. It evokes a deep understanding and revelation of Christ's divine nature, urging believers to recognize Jesus' sacrifice and draw lessons for their own faith.

37.epoque: This verse is set in the first century, at a time when Judaism and Christianity were emerging in a Roman context, marked by religious and political tensions.
37.passage: John 19 describes the crucifixion of Jesus, a culminating moment of His earthly ministry, where He bears the weight of humanity's sins. This verse refers to a prophecy from Zechariah, highlighting the fulfillment of the Scriptures in Christ's passion.
37.culture: In Jewish culture, crucifixion was considered a shame, and piercing someone evoked profound indignity. However, this also highlights the prophetic dimension of the Messiah's suffering, who was expected as a suffering savior.
37.interpretation: The verse emphasizes the duality of Jesus' vision: those who have pierced Him will see Him not only in His suffering but also in His glory. This reminds us that Christ's suffering is the means by which we access redemption and the revelation of His majesty.
37.commentaire: John 19:37 calls us to reflect on our own relationship with Christ. By seeing Him whom we have pierced, we are invited to recognize our part in His sacrifice and to embrace the grace He offers us. This passage encourages us to live in the light of this revelation, witnessing God's love and mercy in our daily lives.

mots.sens: The term 'mathētēs' refers to a disciple, a learner, or a student. In the biblical context, it implies a relationship of learning and following a master, in this case, Jesus. This word emphasizes commitment and devotion, but also the challenges that those who choose to follow Christ may encounter, as shown here by Joseph of Arimathea, who hides his faith for fear of the authorities.

The word 'sōma' means 'body' and refers to the physical reality of the human being. In this verse, it is particularly significant as it underscores the humanity of Jesus, who truly suffered and died. This reminds believers of the importance of the resurrection, as the body of Jesus, though dead, is the same that will be glorified, illustrating the promise of eternal life for those who believe in Him.

The word 'Ioudaios' refers to the Jews, an ethnic and religious group central to the New Testament. In this context, it evokes the tensions between Jesus' disciples and the Jewish authorities. This highlights the risk faced by Joseph of Arimathea as a secret disciple and sheds light on the struggle between fear of man and faith in Christ.

38.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, at a time when Judaism and Christianity were evolving, marked by political and religious tensions. Jesus' disciples faced strong opposition from both Jewish and Roman authorities.
38.passage: This verse is found in the account of Jesus' crucifixion, where Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the Sanhedrin, takes the risk of requesting Jesus' body. This occurs after Jesus' death, a moment of despair and confusion for His disciples.
38.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the body of a condemned person had to be treated with care and respect, which explains Joseph's request. Additionally, the fact that he was a secret disciple underscores the social and religious pressures faced by those who believed in Jesus.
38.interpretation: Joseph of Arimathea represents those who, although fearing the consequences, choose to stand up for their faith. His action of taking Jesus' body is an act of courage and devotion, symbolizing the necessity of witnessing our faith, even in difficult circumstances.
38.commentaire: This verse reminds us that faith may sometimes require courage, especially in the face of opposition. Like Joseph, we are called to be witnesses of Christ, even when it involves risks. By taking care of Jesus' body, he teaches us the importance of valuing and respecting life, even in death, and of living our faith authentically and visibly.

mots.sens: The word 'νύξ' means 'night'. It evokes darkness, both physical and spiritual. In the context of Nicodemus, it symbolizes his hesitation to publicly identify as a disciple of Jesus, highlighting the struggle between the light of truth and the darkness of unbelief. Theologically, this reminds us that many come to Christ in moments of darkness, seeking the light.

The term 'μυρρός' translates to 'myrrh', an aromatic resin used in funeral rites and as perfume. In this verse, it symbolizes the respect and honor that Nicodemus gives to Jesus, even after His death. Spiritually, this reminds us that Jesus is the fragrance of life, and even in death, He is revered and celebrated.

The word 'αλόη' refers to aloe, a plant used for its medicinal and fragrant properties. In the context of Jesus' burial, it represents the care and love that Nicodemus shows towards the body of Christ. Theologically, this reminds us that Jesus, even in death, is surrounded by care and honors, emphasizing His role as Savior.

39.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, at a time when Judaism and Christianity were beginning to distinguish themselves, with increasing tensions between Jewish religious authorities and the followers of Jesus.
39.passage: In John 19, the chapter describes the events surrounding the crucifixion and burial of Jesus. Nicodemus, who had previously visited Jesus at night, shows courage by associating himself with His burial, demonstrating a transformation of his faith.
39.culture: In Jewish culture, burial was a sacred act, and the use of myrrh and aloe for embalming the body was a way to show respect. This also reflects the importance of funeral rites in the society of the time.
39.interpretation: By bringing spices, Nicodemus demonstrates a growing faith and a willingness to associate with Jesus even after His death. This illustrates how faith can manifest in concrete actions, even in difficult circumstances.
39.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of witnessing our faith, even when it seems risky. Like Nicodemus, we are called to honor Jesus in our lives, bringing our 'best offerings' in response to His sacrifice. This encourages us to come out of darkness and live our faith in a visible and committed way.

mots.sens: This word means 'body' and refers to the physical form of a human being. In the context of John 19:40, it emphasizes the humanity of Jesus, who truly suffered and died. It also reminds us of the importance of the resurrection, as the body of Jesus, though dead, will be glorified, thus highlighting the victory over death.

This term means 'to wrap' or 'to clothe'. In this verse, it evokes the care and respect given to the body of Jesus during His burial. It underscores the dignity and love surrounding Christ's death, while also foreshadowing the resurrection where He will be clothed in a glorified body.

This word refers to 'spices' or 'fragrances', used in the burial process. It symbolizes the respect and honor given to the deceased, but in the case of Jesus, it also foreshadows the fragrance of His resurrection and the message of the Gospel that will spread throughout the world.

This term means 'tomb' or 'grave'. In the context of John 19:40, it evokes the place where the body of Jesus was laid, but it is also a symbol of death. The tomb of Jesus has become a place of transformation, as it cannot hold the risen Christ, which is a message of hope for all believers.

40.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during the Roman occupation of Judea, a period marked by religious and political tensions. Jesus is crucified in a context where messianic expectations are high among the Jews.
40.passage: John 19:40 is found at the end of the Gospel of John, where the crucifixion and burial of Jesus are described. This moment is crucial as it precedes the resurrection, highlighting the importance of Jesus' death for the salvation of humanity.
40.culture: In Jewish culture, burial was a sacred act, often accompanied by prayers and rituals. The spices used were also a sign of respect and devotion towards the deceased, showing the disciples' love for Jesus even after His death.
40.interpretation: This verse reminds us that the death of Jesus was real and that He was treated with the respect due to a king. Spiritually, it teaches us that even in death, there is hope of resurrection and eternal life for those who believe in Him.
40.commentaire: The care given to the body of Jesus by His disciples is a powerful testimony of their love and faith. As believers, we are called to honor the sacrifice of Christ and to live in light of His resurrection. This passage encourages us to reflect on our own relationship with death and the hope we have in Christ, who has conquered death.

mots.sens: This word means 'garden' and evokes a cultivated space, often associated with beauty and life. In the biblical context, a garden can symbolize divine creation and intimacy with God, like the Garden of Eden. The presence of a garden at the site of the crucifixion highlights a poignant contrast between death and life, suggesting that the resurrection of Jesus will bring new life.

The term 'tomb' refers to a burial place, often associated with death and separation. In this verse, the fact that it is 'new' and 'where no one had yet been laid' emphasizes the uniqueness of Jesus' resurrection. This means that death cannot claim this place, as Jesus, being the Son of God, has conquered death and offers eternal life.

41.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during the Roman occupation of Judea, a period marked by religious and political tensions. Jesus is crucified in a context where messianic expectations are high among the Jews.
41.passage: John 19 describes the events surrounding the crucifixion of Jesus. This verse specifies the location of His burial, highlighting the importance of this location in the passion and resurrection narrative.
41.culture: In Jewish culture, tombs were often sacred places, and burial was an act of respect towards the deceased. The fact that a new tomb is used for Jesus indicates particular attention to His body and dignity, even in death.
41.interpretation: The garden and the new tomb symbolize the transition from death to life. Jesus, being placed in a tomb where no one had been, foreshadows His resurrection and the hope of eternal life for all who believe in Him.
41.commentaire: This verse reminds us that even in moments of suffering and death, God prepares places of life and resurrection. The presence of the garden and the new tomb encourages us to look beyond immediate circumstances and to hope in the promise of eternal life in Christ. As believers, we are called to live in this hope, knowing that death does not have the final word.

mots.sens: The word 'τάφος' refers to a tomb or sepulcher. It evokes not only the resting place of the dead but also the separation between life and death. In the Christian context, this word takes on a profound spiritual dimension, symbolizing the death of Jesus and the hope of resurrection. The proximity of the sepulcher highlights the urgency and respect for the Jewish rites surrounding death.

The term 'παρασκευή' means preparation, particularly in relation to religious rites and observances. In this verse, it refers to the preparation for the Jewish Sabbath, which required that everything be ready before sunset. This word emphasizes the importance of Jewish laws and traditions, while also highlighting how Jesus fits into these practices.

42.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, at a time when Judaism was the dominant religion in Palestine, and tensions between Jewish and Roman authorities were palpable.
42.passage: This verse concludes the account of the crucifixion of Jesus, marking the end of His earthly ministry and the beginning of His burial. It highlights the fulfillment of prophecies and the importance of preparation for the Sabbath.
42.culture: In Jewish culture, respect for funeral rites and preparation for the Sabbath were essential. The proximity of the sepulcher allowed for the observance of these traditions while honoring the body of Jesus.
42.interpretation: Spiritually, this verse reminds us that the death of Jesus is not the end, but the prelude to resurrection. It also underscores the importance of preparation in our spiritual lives, calling us to be ready for the encounter with Christ.
42.commentaire: This passage teaches us about the necessity of respecting traditions while recognizing their fulfillment in Christ. Just as Jesus was laid in the sepulcher, we are called to lay down our burdens and sins at His feet, knowing that He has triumphed over death. This encourages us to live in the hope of resurrection and to prepare our hearts for the return of the Lord.
